summary: A record 17 spacecraft tracked a coronal mass ejection (CME) that erupted from the sun on December 15, 2024. The observations revealed that the solar eruption was surprisingly lopsided, featuring two asymmetric lobes moving at different speeds. This wide-angle tracking approach provides crucial data for improving space-weather forecasting and protecting future space exploration.
key_points: A record 17 spacecraft tracked and characterized a single coronal mass ejection (CME) from the sun.
The CME featured two asymmetric lobes moving at different speeds, with a faster lobe heading toward Earth and Mars and a slower lobe heading west.
The faster Earth-bound lobe was initially obscured by the larger, slower lobe, demonstrating the value of wide-angle spacecraft positioning.
Understanding and detecting asymmetric CMEs is vital for providing accurate radiation warnings to astronauts during future human space exploration.

title: Europe's Next-Gen Rocket Concept Could Be Way More Efficient Than SpaceX's Starship - BGR
author: Gerard Griessel
content:
Europe's Next-Gen Rocket Concept Could Be Way More Efficient Than SpaceX's Starship
Germany's Aerospace Center (DLR) published a paper in May 2025 proposing a more efficient European version of SpaceX's Starship rocket, with the concept called the RLV C5. The team from DLR studied SpaceX's publicly available data and provided a unique assessment of the rocket's ability. The analysis was built on telemetry data obtained via public broadcasts from SpaceX, which was logged by a text recognition algorithm. The aim of the study is to provide a competitive launch platform for Europe. The key improvement that this team aims to deliver is up to 74% of its mass as payload to low earth orbit, compared to Starship which delivers 40% of its mass to orbit. If accomplished, this would represent a significant advantage over Starship.
By studying the launch data, the team developed an entirely different concept, proposing a design that is similar to that of the Space Shuttle, with a twist. SpaceX's Starship separates from the Super Heavy booster, which lands back at the launch site by firing its Raptor engines. The rocket is then caught by the launch tower's Mechazilla arms, a feat which may change everything about space travel. This landing technique costs extra fuel in order to ensure that the rocket can reduce its speed after reentry and come to a powered hover before being caught.
The team from Europe proposes a rocket that is similarly sized to the Starship, but has a SpaceLiner booster with built-in wings that can be used to glide it, before being caught by a subsonic aircraft mid-air. This SpaceLiner booster concept has been in development since 2005. The RLV C5 also proposes to use liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, which are more efficient than the methane and oxygen combination used by Starship.
The RLV C5 has a long way to go
While the concept from the DLR is certainly thought-provoking and innovative, building and flying a rocket of this scale is an enormous undertaking. The biggest problem with the RLV C5 design is that it is still in a conceptual phase, and a lot would have to happen in a short space of time for the idea to take off. The other problem is that SpaceX has set a new bar for the pace of development, so much so that it treats its rocket launches like software updates, rapidly iterating and improving after every test.
By the time the design can see serious investment or production, SpaceX may have improved its own design to such an extent that the European design may already be behind. Since the SpaceLiner concept has never made it into actual production in the 20 years since it was first thought up, it's difficult to imagine the idea taking off. While the team from DLR would be able to lean on key learnings derived from SpaceX's Starship program, developing and building a rocket of this scale would take years to complete. Those charged with the task would have to develop an entirely new rocket with its own heat-shield, rocket engines, and validated gliding performance. Those three concepts were at the center of the Space Shuttle's development hurdles, and required significant funding and time to get right.
Europe's current orbital space initiatives
Europe's most established space launch operator is Arianespace, which Amazon is currently using as its secret weapon to compete with SpaceX's Starlink. The company is a multi-national enterprise flying regular launches out of its Guiana Space Center, using the latest Ariane 6 rocket. While the company has a long history of flying unmanned satellite launches to orbit, even the latest iteration of the Ariane rocket is fully expendable, not offering nearly as much cost efficiency as SpaceX does with its current Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets.
A slew of smaller launch enterprises are developing under the European Space Agency's European Launcher Challenge initiative. However, only one of these companies has made an orbital launch attempt. Isar Aerospace is a German launch provider that launched its Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in Norway for the first time in March 2025. Even though the rocket failed on the first launch, the company is likely to offer future launch capabilities to compete with Arianespace.
The most innovative company to watch in Europe is MaiaSpace, a subsidiary of ArianeGroup, which intends to launch a two-stage reusable rocket called Maia. This rocket aims to use the same reusability concept seen on the SpaceX Falcon 9, and intends to launch its first test flight either this year or next.
summary: Germany's Aerospace Center published a paper proposing the RLV C5, a next-generation European rocket concept aimed at outperforming SpaceX's Starship in payload efficiency. The design utilizes a SpaceLiner booster with wings to glide before being caught mid-air by a subsonic aircraft, alongside a liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen propellant combination. However, the concept remains in the early planning stages, facing significant development hurdles and rapid iteration competition from SpaceX.
key_points: Germany's Aerospace Center proposed the RLV C5 rocket concept to provide a competitive European launch platform.
The RLV C5 aims to deliver up to 74% of its mass as payload to low Earth orbit, compared to Starship's 40%.
The proposed design features a winged booster that glides and is caught mid-air by a subsonic aircraft, utilizing liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
The RLV C5 is currently only in a conceptual phase, having to overcome major hurdles like heat-shield and engine development.
European space initiatives also include Arianespace's expendable Ariane 6, Isar Aerospace's Spectrum, and MaiaSpace's reusable Maia rocket.

title: Jean Paton, botanist and leading authority on liverworts of the British Isles
author: Telegraph Obituaries
content:
![Jean Paton](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499033415_17874823140900_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGxjY7D4-DvNKzsaeMBkg_BrbH1Njtb0ulsvf5cZdBSU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Jean Paton](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499033415_17874823140900_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqGxjY7D4-DvNKzsaeMBkg_BrbH1Njtb0ulsvf5cZdBSU.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Jean Paton, who has died aged 97, was a botanist specialising in the study of mosses, liverworts and hornworts, a discipline known as bryology.
Of about 20,000 bryophyte species known worldwide, approximately 1,100 have been recorded in Britain, which is around 58 per cent of all the species known in Europe. Though often without distinction to the untrained eye, they can be structurally complex. The scientist and polymath Robert Hooke described what “common moss” looked like under the microscope in his 1665 book Micrographia, noting that it “may compare for the beauty of it with any Plant that grows”.
On that point Jean Paton was in firm agreement. An early, “thrilling” encounter with several mosses on a woodland floor in Wales ignited a passion that developed into a 70-year career. On her mission to compile a comprehensive catalogue of liverworts, she travelled across England, Wales, Scotland, the Isle of Man, the Hebrides, the Isles of Scilly and the Channel Islands.
One of the most prolific recorders of bryological specimens in the last half-century, she described several species new to science, including Telaranea murphyae, Plagiochila britannica and the moss Ditrichum comubicum.
Her magnum opus, The Liverwort Flora of the British Isles (1999), took 30 years to come to fruition. At more than 600 pages, it was hailed as the definitive modern work on the subject. Illustrated by Jean Paton’s own line drawings, it was “a Rolls-Royce of floras”, in the words of one reviewer, “invaluable to European bryologists, and even of relevance to workers as far afield as North America and Japan”. In 2003 Jean Paton was appointed MBE for services to biology and nature conservation.
She was born Jean Annette Comyn on January 4 1929. Mild dyslexia and poor teaching at five different schools meant that she did not learn to read by herself until she was nine years old. Her early interest in wildflowers was nurtured by her mother, who gave her a copy of Fitch & Smith’s Illustrations of the British Flora. Jean taught herself to paint and draw them and studied botany at Bedford College in London.
![Jean Paton and her 2022 book](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/obituaries/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000499033415_17874824275360_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqmOKpe7YStN95arEmpvBAWaKJOu9-QIiF6XqgXdUIMtc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
On a summer job in the Lake District in 1950 she was shown a collection of shoeboxes containing bryophytes collected throughout the area and given the task of naming them. “I suddenly realised this was fun,” she recalled, “rather like following up clues in a detective story.”
In the summer of 1952 she became a research and herbarium assistant in the Southampton University Botany Department. Soon she was searching for bryophytes in her native Southampton and linking her records to the National Grid system, allowing her discoveries to be published based on hectads, or 10-km grid squares.
Following her marriage to Valentine “Pat” Paton, an architect and ardent naturalist, she moved to Probus, Cornwall, in 1959 and embarked on two books, Wild Flowers in Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly and Flowers of the Cornish Coast. In 2000 she received an award from the Linnean Society for the illustrations in The Liverwort Flora of the British Isles.
Subsequent books included Magnolias in Cornish Gardens (2001, with her husband Pat) and Bryophyte Flora of the Isles of Scilly (2005, with David Holyoak). Her additional research was published as A Supplement to the Liverwort Flora of the British Isles in 2022.
Jean Paton was vice-president and president of the British Bryological Society from 1974 to 1977; she was appointed an honorary member of the society in 1984. Her herbarium, heavily weighted in favour of liverworts, was added to the collections of the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh in 1998.
Her husband died in 2012.
Jean Paton, born January 4 1929, died August 10 2026
summary: Jean Paton, who has died at the age of 97, was a leading botanist and bryologist renowned for her extensive fieldwork and research on mosses, liverworts, and hornworts. Over a 70-year career, she traveled extensively across the British Isles to catalogue specimens and described several species new to science. Her career culminated in her 1999 magnum opus, The Liverwort Flora of the British Isles, which established her as a preeminent authority in her field and earned her an MBE in 2003.
key_points: Jean Paton specialized in bryology, focusing on mosses, liverworts, and hornworts during a 70-year career.
She authored The Liverwort Flora of the British Isles in 1999, a 600-page definitive work illustrated with her own line drawings.
She described several species new to science, including Telaranea murphyae, Plagiochila britannica, and the moss Ditrichum comubicum.
She served as vice-president and president of the British Bryological Society from 1974 to 1977 and was appointed an MBE in 2003.

title: When scientists announced Webb’s first definitive detection of Neptune’s auroras in March 2025, they revealed another surprise: observations taken in 2023 showed that the planet’s upper atmosphere had cooled by several hundred degrees since Voyager 2 visited in 1989—and scientists still don’t know exactly why.
author: Space Daily; Lachlan Brown
content:
The first definitive detection of auroras on Neptune came with a quieter discovery concealed in the same infrared spectrum. When the James Webb Space Telescope observed the distant planet in June 2023, it found the molecular signature astronomers had pursued for decades. It also found an upper atmosphere far colder than the one Voyager 2 measured during its 1989 flyby.
The auroras made the image. The temperature made the puzzle.
When NASA and the research team announced the result on 26 March 2025, the comparison was striking. Webb measured about 358 kelvin. Voyager’s best estimate had been around 750 kelvin. Even after allowing for the different instruments and atmospheric layers involved, the gap remained much too large to dismiss as a change of thermometer.
That does not mean scientists watched Neptune cool steadily for 34 years. They have two widely separated snapshots, made in different ways. What they can say is narrower and still surprising: the thin gas high above Neptune’s clouds was several hundred degrees cooler in 2023 than it appeared to be in 1989, and no one yet has a complete explanation.
Webb found a chemical fingerprint, not a blue-green light show
Webb observed Neptune on 22 June 2023 with its Near-Infrared Spectrograph, NIRSpec. Rather than merely photographing the planet, the instrument separated its light by wavelength across different points on the disc. In that spectrum, researchers identified clear emission from H3+, a molecule made from three hydrogen nuclei and two electrons.
H3+ forms when energetic particles ionise molecular hydrogen and the resulting chemistry rearranges the atoms. On Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus, it is an established tracer of auroral activity. Neptune had been the holdout. Voyager 2 detected radio emissions associated with the planet’s magnetic environment and returned suggestive ultraviolet observations, but not the decisive H3+ signature.
The cyan patches in NASA’s published Webb composite are a map of that infrared emission layered over images of Neptune. They are not a literal representation of what a person hovering near the planet would see. The colour makes the signal legible to us; the spectrum is what makes the detection convincing.
Neptune puts its auroras in unexpected places
On Earth, people learn to associate auroras with the far north and south. Neptune does not arrange its magnetism so neatly. Its magnetic field is tilted by about 47 degrees relative to its rotation axis, and the field is also offset from the planet’s centre. Geographic north and magnetic north are therefore very different directions.
Webb’s strongest H3+ enhancements appeared around southern mid-latitudes, rather than forming a familiar cap over the geographic pole. That location fits a world whose magnetic axis swings through space at an extreme angle as Neptune rotates every 16 hours or so.
This geometry matters beyond the appearance of an aurora. It determines where charged particles can be channelled into the atmosphere, where they deposit energy, and how local heating might be distributed around the planet. An auroral map is also a rough map of the forces acting on the upper atmosphere.
Two thermometers, 34 years apart
The study published in Nature Astronomy derived an H3+ temperature of 358 plus or minus 8 kelvin. That is about 85 degrees Celsius. Voyager 2’s ultraviolet solar-occultation measurement in 1989 yielded an exospheric temperature near 750 plus or minus 150 kelvin, about 477 degrees Celsius at the central estimate.
Temperatures expressed in Celsius can sound misleading here. Neptune’s upper atmosphere is so rarefied that it contains very little heat in the everyday sense. A molecule may be moving at a speed corresponding to a high kinetic temperature while the gas remains far too thin to warm a person or a spacecraft as dense air would.
The more important caution concerns comparability. Voyager inferred the temperature of the exosphere from the way ultraviolet sunlight passed through the atmosphere. Webb inferred a temperature from the distribution of H3+ emission lines lower down. They did not put the same instrument at the same altitude on the same date.
The researchers addressed that difference with an atmospheric model. It indicated that the H3+ temperature should be less than 10 per cent below the equivalent Voyager-style exospheric temperature. That correction is meaningful, but nowhere near enough to bridge a central-value gap of almost 400 kelvin. Their conclusion was that Neptune’s ionosphere really was considerably hotter during the Voyager encounter.
It is best described as a change between two epochs, not as a measured cooling rate. The atmosphere could have risen, fallen or fluctuated in between. There are no annual readings hiding behind the headline.
The colder atmosphere may explain a decades-long failure
Before Webb, astronomers had repeatedly searched for Neptune’s H3+ emission from the ground without a firm detection. Those attempts were shaped partly by the hot atmosphere Voyager found. If Neptune remained near 750 kelvin, its H3+ should have radiated more strongly in the infrared and might have been within reach.
But H3+ emission is strongly sensitive to temperature. At roughly 358 kelvin, the ion radiates much more weakly. The auroral chemistry could therefore be present while its most useful infrared beacon sat below earlier detection limits.
Webb had the sensitivity and spectral coverage to pull that faint structure from Neptune’s light. The NASA account of the discovery describes both the relief of finally seeing the signal and the surprise of finding such a cold ionosphere. In this case, a nondetection over many years did not mean the phenomenon was absent. The atmosphere had made its evidence harder to see.
A Neptunian season is nearly as long as the gap
Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun, so each season lasts roughly four decades. The 34 years between Voyager and Webb are almost a season, which makes seasonal change an obvious suspect. Yet the paper argues that season alone does not settle the problem. Changes of this size can occur on timescales shorter than Neptune’s full seasonal rhythm, and the planet does not experience the extreme seasonal geometry of Uranus.
A simple solar-cycle answer is also unsatisfying. The level of solar ultraviolet activity was broadly comparable around the two observations. Neptune is about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth, and predicting the solar wind there is difficult. The researchers note that Webb’s visit may have coincided with one of the stronger modeled increases in solar-wind dynamic pressure during 2023, but the estimated arrival time carries uncertainty measured in weeks.
That leaves several plausible contributors without a settled division of responsibility. Charged particles guided by Neptune’s magnetic field can heat the auroral atmosphere. Waves rising from lower layers may carry energy upward. The solar wind can compress and disturb the magnetosphere. Material arriving from the rings or elsewhere in the Neptune system may alter ionospheric chemistry and cooling.
These are mechanisms to test, not a list from which one has already been chosen.
The atmosphere is cold only by comparison
Even at 358 kelvin, Neptune’s upper atmosphere is warmer than sunlight alone should make it. The researchers estimate that absorbed solar energy would support a temperature closer to 130 kelvin. Explaining the remaining difference is part of the long-running giant-planet upper-atmosphere energy problem: how do these remote worlds move enough energy into their thin outer layers?
This is related to, but distinct from, the question in Space Daily’s recent examination of Neptune’s hidden heat and its contrast with Uranus. That comparison concerns the planet’s overall energy budget and the heat escaping from its deep interior. The Webb result concerns the thermosphere and ionosphere, extremely tenuous layers far above the visible clouds.
A planet can release more internal energy than it absorbs from sunlight while its upper atmosphere cools between observations. Heat must still be transported through many layers, and magnetospheric energy can be deposited from above. Treating every temperature at Neptune as one shared thermostat would erase the very physics researchers are trying to isolate.
Cooling changes the size of the upper atmosphere
The result is not only about a number on a temperature scale. Hot gas expands. Cooler gas is held more tightly by gravity. According to the study, a fall from around 750 to around 350 kelvin would reduce the atmospheric scale height by more than a factor of two.
Scale height describes how quickly atmospheric density falls with altitude. A smaller value means Neptune’s upper atmosphere is more compact. That affects models of how ring particles spiral inward, where infalling material encounters drag, and what a future spacecraft might meet above the clouds.
It also changes the context for old data. Voyager’s hot upper atmosphere cannot automatically be treated as Neptune’s permanent baseline. A single flyby produces exquisite detail at one moment, but it can turn weather, magnetospheric activity or another temporary state into what later generations mistake for a fixed planetary property.
The next Webb visit can test change rather than memory
The team wants repeated observations over the Sun’s roughly 11-year activity cycle. Webb can measure the H3+ spectrum again, map where the emission brightens, and see whether its temperature changes with solar-wind conditions or auroral intensity. A run of observations would begin to separate a long trend from short-lived variability.
Voyager 2 is still the only spacecraft to have visited Neptune. It passed about 4,800 kilometres above the planet’s north polar region on 25 August 1989, gathered its close measurements, and continued outward. The mission’s brief encounter remains foundational, but it was never designed to watch an entire Neptunian season.
Webb cannot sample plasma in place or orbit Neptune’s magnetic field. What it can do is return. That ability turns Voyager’s historic snapshot into the first point in a much longer comparison.
The auroral detection closed one search and immediately made the temperature discrepancy harder to ignore. Neptune’s upper atmosphere was much cooler when Webb looked than when Voyager passed, yet it was still far warmer than sunlight alone can explain. Somewhere between solar wind, magnetic geometry, atmospheric waves, chemistry and the planet below lies the missing energy accounting. For now, the honest result is not a tidy cause. It is a much better measurement of how much remains unknown.
summary: Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have made the first definitive detection of auroras on Neptune by observing the molecular signature H3+ in June 2023. Alongside this discovery, researchers found that Neptune's upper atmosphere has cooled significantly—dropping from about 750 kelvin during Voyager 2's 1989 flyby to roughly 358 kelvin in 2023. Scientists currently lack a complete explanation for this massive temperature drop, noting that factors like seasons and solar cycles do not fully account for the change.
key_points: Webb detected H3+ emissions on Neptune, confirming auroral activity that previously eluded ground-based telescopes.
Measurements indicate Neptune's upper atmosphere was hundreds of degrees cooler in 2023 than when Voyager 2 measured it in 1989.
Neptune's magnetic field is heavily tilted and offset, causing its strongest auroral enhancements to appear around southern mid-latitudes rather than at the geographic poles.
The significant cooling reduces Neptune's atmospheric scale height by more than a factor of two, meaning the upper atmosphere is now much more compact.

title: China postpones launch of unprecedented water-hunting moon mission amid space race | CNN
author: Jackie Wattles; Simone McCarthy
content:
The highly anticipated launch of China’s robotic Chang’e-7 mission, designed to scour the moon’s south pole for water ice — a highly valuable resource that the US also hopes to use — “cannot take place during the planned window this year,” according to a statement from the China Manned Space Engineering Office shared by Chinese state media.
The mission had been expected to lift off as soon as Sunday evening, or Monday morning Beijing time. It’s not clear how soon China may be able to attempt to get the mission off the ground.
The precise reason for the delay was not immediately clear. State media shared only that the “lunar probe does not meet launch conditions,” and the “assessment was conducted following the principle of prudence, reliability and absolute mission success.”
The United States and China are racing to build settlements on the moon’s south pole, where water is believed to exist in frozen abundance inside shadowy craters.
No mission has yet directly analyzed water on the moon, as Chang’e-7 will attempt to do.
Though the US has detected and begun estimating the size of water ice stores using remote sensors on orbiting satellites, it has never successfully sent a probe to drill for the resource.
One Texas-based company, Intuitive Machines, sent a water-hunting drill to the moon in 2025, but the spacecraft tripped while attempting to land on the south pole’s notorious treacherous terrain and could not complete its mission objectives.
But Chang’e-7’s launch delay could put this chapter of the space race — as US officials have referred to the standoff with China — back on competitive footing.
Race to the south pole
The US has several spacecraft heading for the same lunar region as Chang’e-7 is targeting within the next year. Pittsburgh-based company Astrobotic Technologies could launch its Griffin lander to the moon’s south pole as soon as late 2026. And Jeff Bezos’ space venture, Blue Origin, has plans to send up to two robotic landers to the moon next year, one of which may include the VIPER rover, a prospecting robot specifically designed by NASA to hunt for water ice and other lunar resources.
The belief that the lunar south pole contains vast stores of frozen water is a key reason this region has become the main stage for this international competition. The resource holds enormous value for deep-space exploration and a potential lunar base because it can be converted to breathable air, drinking water or even rocket fuel.
Whether water ice is present in sufficient amounts to be useful for these purposes is not currently known, and Chang’e-7 could help make “important progress on this question, sharpening and focusing experiments for further exploration and testing,” Yuqi Qian, a lunar geologist at the University of Hong Kong, told CNN.
Qian said that with Chang’e-7, China’s lunar program is “shifting from an exploration program to a resource utilization program.”
summary: China has postponed the launch of its Chang'e-7 lunar south pole mission because the probe currently does not meet launch conditions. The unprecedented mission aimed to scour the moon for water ice, a critical resource for future lunar settlements that the United States is also targeting. The exact reason for the delay remains unclear, though state media noted the decision was made out of caution and reliability.
key_points: China postponed the Chang'e-7 moon mission, which was originally planned for launch within this year's window.
State media reported the delay because the lunar probe did not meet launch conditions.
The US and China are engaged in a space race to build settlements at the moon's south pole to access water ice.
No mission has yet successfully drilled for or directly analyzed water on the moon.
The US has multiple spacecraft, including NASA's VIPER rover via Blue Origin, planned for the lunar south pole region.

title: Light travels from the Sun to Earth in just eight minutes, but the journey from the Sun’s core to its surface can take up to 500,000 years
author: Rodielon Putol
content:
![The Sun rises over Earth, as seen from orbit](https://www.earth.com/assets/_next/image/?url=%2Fimg%2F16x9%2F1920%2Fmedia-2026%2F2026%2F08%2F21105050%2Fearth-sunlight-photons-travel-time_1m.jpg&w=1920&q=75)
Light travels from the Sun to Earth in just eight minutes, but the journey from the Sun’s core to its surface can take up to 500,000 years
The sunlight reaching Earth from the Sun's visible surface crosses space in about 8 minutes. Before that, however, the radiant energy that ultimately emerges as sunlight can spend…
![Rodielon Putol](https://www.earth.com/assets/_next/image/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcff2.earth.com%2Fuploads%2F2024%2F03%2F04053136%2Frodielon-putol-earth-writer-headshot-712x1000.jpg&w=96&q=75)
The sunlight reaching Earth from the Sun’s visible surface crosses space in about 8 minutes. Before that, however, the radiant energy that ultimately emerges as sunlight can spend an extraordinarily long time moving outward through the Sun’s dense interior.
A widely cited calculation published in 1992 estimated a photon-diffusion timescale of about 170,000 years for the present Sun. That figure describes a statistical transport process, not one unchanged photon surviving from the solar core to your skin.
Light moves by diffusion
The Sun’s interior is made of extremely hot plasma, composed largely of ionized hydrogen and helium along with free electrons. Deep inside the Sun, matter is so dense that radiation cannot simply stream outward as it does once it reaches space.
Photons interact repeatedly with matter through processes that include absorption, re-emission, and scattering. Each interaction changes the route taken by radiant energy, so its outward progress resembles a random walk rather than a straight path.
A random walk can involve enormous motion while producing only modest net progress. A photon may travel a short distance, interact with matter, and then continue in a direction that is partly sideways or even back toward the core.
This repeated interaction is especially important in the radiative zone, where radiation is the main mechanism carrying energy outward. Farther from the center, convection becomes increasingly important in moving energy toward the solar surface.
Random walks change the math
The basic random-walk relationship is often summarized by saying that net displacement grows roughly with the square root of the number of steps. Reaching a distance R with an average step length l therefore requires a number of steps that scales approximately as (R/l)^2.
That is different from saying that the distance traveled is the square of the number of steps. The original calculation confused those quantities, leading to an incorrect description of both the number of interactions and the total path length.
The average step length also cannot be treated as a single fixed value everywhere inside the Sun. Density, temperature, and opacity change strongly with depth, so the distance radiation can travel before another interaction varies through the solar interior.
R. Mitalas and K. R. Sills addressed this issue using step lengths derived from a solar model. They found an average step length of about 0.035 inches (0.090 centimeters), substantially shorter than the 0.2- to 0.4-inch (0.5- to 1.0-centimeter) values commonly used in earlier simplified estimates.
The 170,000-year estimate
With the shorter average step length, Mitalas and Sills calculated a photon-diffusion timescale of about 170,000 years for the present Sun. Their paper was published in The Astrophysical Journal in December 1992.
The result did not come from a recent, sophisticated simulation, as the original version suggested. It came from a simple random-walk treatment combined with step lengths determined from a solar model.
The 170,000-year figure should therefore be presented as a model-based photon-diffusion estimate rather than a precisely measured travel time. The calculation describes the statistical diffusion of radiation through the Sun’s interior.
It also does not support an accepted range extending from 170,000 to more than 500,000 years. No peer-reviewed source supporting the 500,000-year figure in the original article was identified.
Photons do not stay intact
There is another important limitation to the familiar story of a photon “escaping” the Sun. Photons can be absorbed, and energy can later be emitted again in new photons with different energies and directions.
For that reason, the visible photon that eventually leaves the photosphere should not be imagined as the same individual photon originally produced by a nuclear reaction in the core.
The random-walk picture tracks the diffusion of radiation and energy through matter, not the uninterrupted biography of a single particle.
Energy generated in the core also changes form as it moves outward. High-energy radiation interacting with the solar plasma is repeatedly redistributed, and the spectrum that ultimately emerges from the photosphere is very different from the radiation associated with fusion reactions deep inside the Sun.
Once a visible photon escapes the photosphere, the situation changes dramatically. Space between the Sun and Earth is transparent enough that the photon can cover roughly 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) in about 8 minutes.
Human history comparison
A timescale of 170,000 years is still immense on a human scale. Neanderthals lived from roughly 400,000 to 40,000 years ago, so a 170,000-year diffusion timescale overlaps a period when Neanderthals were present.
It is not, however, older than Homo sapiens as a species. Fossil evidence places Homo sapiens at about 300,000 years ago, with important early remains from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco dating to roughly that period.
The safer comparison is therefore that the 170,000-year estimate reaches back to a time when both Neanderthals and Homo sapiens already existed. Saying that the sunlight reaching us began its journey before Homo sapiens appeared is not supported by this estimate.
Limits of the estimate
Photon diffusion inside a star is a model of statistical energy transport through matter whose properties change dramatically with radius. A simple random-walk analogy is useful for explaining the basic idea, but it cannot reproduce every detail of radiative transfer inside the Sun.
The original article’s claim that a mean free path below 0.039 inches (1 millimeter) was established by “more recent research” is also misleading.
Mitalas and Sills reported an average value of 0.035 inches (0.090 centimeters) in 1992, and that shorter step length led them to the 170,000-year result.
No peer-reviewed source was identified for the claim that a shorter mean free path pushes the crossing time above 500,000 years. That figure has therefore been removed rather than presented as part of an accepted scientific range.
The central point remains striking without exaggeration. Radiation can diffuse through the dense solar interior for a very long time, while a photon that has escaped the Sun can cross interplanetary space to Earth in only about 8 minutes.
The photon-diffusion estimate was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

summary: While light from the Sun's surface reaches Earth in about eight minutes, radiant energy takes an immense amount of time to travel outward through the dense solar interior. A widely cited 1992 study by R. Mitalas and K. R. Sills estimated a photon-diffusion timescale of roughly 170,000 years using a random-walk model. This process involves repeated absorption, scattering, and re-emission rather than a single uninterrupted photon journey.
key_points: Sunlight crosses the space between the Sun and Earth in approximately eight minutes.
A 1992 study published in The Astrophysical Journal estimated a photon-diffusion timescale of about 170,000 years for the Sun's interior.
Energy moves outward through the dense plasma via a random-walk process involving repeated absorption, scattering, and re-emission.
The 170,000-year timescale overlaps with the existence of Neanderthals and Homo sapiens, but is not older than Homo sapiens as a species.
No peer-reviewed source supports an extended crossing time of 500,000 years.

title: Artemis II crew to receive top US space medal for historic lunar journey
author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
content:
The crew of the historic Artemis II lunar flyby mission have earned the US’s top space medal, officials have announced.
Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen are set to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August, the US space agency Nasa said.
Nasa’s website indicates that only 30 astronauts have gained the honor – among them Neil Armstrong, the first person to walk on the moon, and John Glenn, who was first to orbit Earth and then served four terms in the US Senate.
Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen were selected for the medal, despite its name, by Donald Trump after the Nasa administrator, Jared Isaacman, recommended them to the president.
The Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for farthest distance traveled from Earth during their 10-day mission, which began on 1 April. They reached 252,756 miles (406,771km) as they swung above the lunar surface, surpassing the 1970 record of 248,655 miles as part of US plans to again land on the moon – then eventually reach Mars.
“This was not easy,” Wiseman said to reporters after the Artemis II mission safely ended with a textbook splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. “Before you launch, it feels like it’s the greatest dream on Earth. And when you’re out there, you just want to get back to your families and your friends. It’s a special thing to be a human, and it’s a special thing to be on planet Earth.”
The medal ceremony scheduled for Wiseman and his colleagues at the Johnson Space Center in Houston comes four months after Trump hosted the Artemis II crew at the White House. The occasion was marked in part by the president, who turned 80 in June, telling the astronauts: “I would have had no trouble making it – I’m physically very, very good.”
Nasa listed an 11am start time for the ceremony, with a video live stream of the event available at www.nasa.gov/live.
Trump has sought to embrace the Artemis II crew’s achievements despite his administration’s proposal to cut Nasa’s budget by 23%, including a 46% reduction for space science initiatives, for the 2027 fiscal year beginning on 1 October. A House commerce, justice and science subcommittee led by Trump’s Republican party responded by advancing its own Nasa budget proposal that would maintain the science projects the president has been aiming to eliminate.
Beside Armstrong and Glenn, previous Congressional Space Medal of Honor recipients include astronauts who were killed in the Apollo I fire as well as the explosions of the Challenger and Columbia space shuttles.
Douglas Hurley and Robert Behnken were the last astronauts to have been chosen for the medal before the Artemis II crew. Hurley and Behnken in 2020 became the first to launch into orbit on a commercial spacecraft, and they accepted the medal in 2023 during Joe Biden’s presidency.
summary: The four-person Artemis II crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August at the Johnson Space Center. Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen were selected for the honor after breaking the Apollo 13 record for the farthest distance traveled from Earth during their April lunar flyby mission. They join an exclusive group of only 30 previous recipients to earn the US's top space medal.
key_points: The Artemis II crew consists of Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen.
The crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor on 28 August at the Johnson Space Center in Houston.
During their 10-day mission starting 1 April, the crew reached 252,756 miles from Earth, breaking the 1970 Apollo 13 record.
Only 30 astronauts have previously received the medal, including Neil Armstrong and John Glenn.

title: 'A winter run left me dead on a mountainside'
author: Sarah Ingram
content:
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/tommy-price-a-winter-run-left-me-dead-on-a-mountainside.png?w=646) 
Tommy Price remembers nothing of the day he was found face down in the snow on a mountain with no heartbeat.
He doesn’t remember getting dressed in his leggings, jacket, snood and beanie that morning, or running 28 miles of a 30-mile route over Skiddaw and Great Calva in the Lake District.
He doesn’t remember his legs freezing up or trying to skid down a rocky path until his backside bled in 2022.
Tommy was fit, healthy and 26 when he and his friend Max set out to run the legendary fell-running trail the Bob Graham Round in Cumbria on a grey, snowy January morning. A former basketball player and bodybuilder, he was in excellent physical condition and had plenty of mountain running experience when they set off.
‘I can’t remember anything of the run. The mountain rescue doctor said it was like a Word document that doesn’t have autosave when there is a power cut.
‘He thinks I will never remember the day of the accident,’ says Tommy, now 31. His last memory is of parking up in Keswick.
It was 0°C in Cumbria that day, but between minus 15°C and minus 20°C higher up with the wind chill. Tommy and Max had also run through a river, making them much colder, he tells Metro from his home in Huddersfield.
‘Max later told me that as I was running up Blencathra I started dropping to my knees and saying I couldn’t carry on. He kept picking me up and I kept saying I wanted to turn around. That’s when the hypothermia set in. I was delirious.’
As Max ran back and forth trying to keep himself warm while helping his friend, Tommy’s legs stopped working and he started sliding down the mountain, ‘ripping my bum open’. Later, doctors told him he was lucky not to need skin grafts.
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
With their mobile phones out of battery, they were about a mile from a farm when Tommy’s legs seized up and he could go no further. Max wrapped him in an emergency survival bag before running downhill to call 999 and Mountain Rescue.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308551559-73ed-e1786971961921.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘When they got to me, my survival bag was empty and I was 100 metres up the mountain, face down in the snow. They rolled me over and started doing CPR. Then another responder came and gave me the defibrillator.
‘They gave me three electric shocks and I was in ventricular fibrillation, so I had no heartbeat. My heart wouldn’t work because I was too cold.
‘It was a bit of a shock for them to find a dead person on the mountain. I think they thought they would give me a Snickers and walk me back down.’
With Max kept safe and warm in a rescue van below, Keswick Mountain Rescue Team volunteers Donald Ferguson and Jonny Hume did everything they could to save Tommy.
Team doctor John Ferris later said that becoming so cold before his heart stopped probably helped save Tommy’s life, as the freezing temperatures protected his brain and other organs from permanent damage.
Rescuers carried out manual CPR for an hour and a half before paramedics were able to use a LUCAS machine, which provides mechanical chest compressions, as Tommy was flown by helicopter to the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle, where life support had been prepared.
As they arrived, the machine ran out of battery and Dr Ferris had to resume manual CPR.
‘I think everybody thought I wasn’t going to make it,’ says Tommy. ‘John Ferris said that in the taxi home from the hospital, after he left me there, he rang Dr Les Gordon, consultant anaesthetist at University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay and team doctor for Langdale and Ambleside Mountain Rescue Team, who said there was a slim chance that I would survive – because nobody survives profound hypothermia.’
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308551562-46b0.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
Profound hypothermia is a life-threatening medical emergency in which the body’s core temperature falls below around 28°C, causing the body’s vital functions to begin shutting down.
At hospital, Tommy was placed on an ECMO machine, a form of advanced life support that temporarily takes over the function of the heart and lungs by pumping blood outside the body, adding oxygen, removing carbon dioxide and returning the blood to the patient, allowing the organs time to rest and recover.
Meanwhile, Max contacted his friend’s family, who were told he had suffered a cardiac arrest and had been taken to hospital. By the time a police officer arrived at his parents’ home to deliver the news, they were already preparing to travel to Newcastle. They gathered at Tommy’s bedside alongside his brothers, David and Gareth.
‘The doctors told them the risks of ECMO. They said, “It will save his life, but it could also kill him.” It was torture for my family because if I survived, they didn’t know if I would have brain damage,’ explains Tommy.
‘They did a CT scan on the third day to see if I had any blood clots in my brain and there was nothing. The doctor said that was a good sign, but the only way to find out was when I woke up. It was a waiting game.’
He regained consciousness after five days in an induced coma. He doesn’t remember waking up – his earliest memory was of a male nurse feeding him water using a sponge.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308551480-e59b-e1786972290798.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘I had a tube down my throat so my swallow reflex was weird. It was very sore. And I remember my brother David feeding me a grape, but I was sick straight away.’
At first, Tommy assumed he had been in a car crash until his family and Max explained what had happened. There was no brain damage.
‘I was scared that I would never walk again, but I was relieved I had survived. Doctors suggested I might need mobility aids around the house.
’I had nerve damage in my hands and feet so I couldn’t grip or pinch anything.
‘I could just about brush my teeth, but I had no strength in my hands. I couldn’t tie my shoelaces, open a can of pop, turn on the shower or drive. I could use my phone, but it took me a long time to write a text message.
‘It was like being a baby again. I needed a lot of help. My parents didn’t know if I would ever recover.’
The nerve damage, which felt like constant pins and needles, is permanent, although the symptoms have disappeared and he has regained full mobility. The only lasting effect is that his hands become cold much more quickly than before.
After three weeks, Tommy left hospital. Remarkably, just nine months after his heart stopped on the mountainside, he completed the London Marathon in three hours and 10 minutes, raising £10,000 for Keswick Mountain Rescue.
Psychologically, Tommy says he has been left unscarred.
‘I just don’t let it get me down,’ he says matter-of-factly.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308551570-291a-e1786972360547.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
‘I look at life positively. It has changed my outlook a little bit. I’m not scared of death. It happens. People don’t believe me when I tell them I’ve died before.’
- 
	![Young woman in bed with her arms by her head](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_307896638-cbfc.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0px%2C0px%2C2500px%2C1406px&resize=646%2C363)
- My childhood babysitter and I are having sex – my parents will be so mad if they find out
- Dirty hotel sex made up for this big disappointment after 10 years of marriage
- Iconic '90s chocolate bar with controversial past makes its return to Asda's shelves
He’s since returned to fell running with gusto, although he avoids doing it in bad weather. A year after his accident, Tommy completed a 120km race in the Brecon Beacons and has entered other ultra-endurance events.
‘I think my fitness kept me alive. The month before my accident we did a 56-mile run and I completed an Ironman that summer, so I was at peak fitness. I’m the fittest I’ve ever been now,’ he adds.
Tommy has since set up his own dog-walking business, which sees him cover around 100km every week.
‘I can’t thank John Ferris, Jonny and Donald enough. They saved my life – and they are all volunteers. If it weren’t for them, I wouldn’t be here today.’
summary: In 2022, 26-year-old Tommy Price suffered profound hypothermia and a cardiac arrest while running the Bob Graham Round in the Lake District with a friend. Keswick Mountain Rescue volunteers and medical teams performed CPR and used advanced life support, including an ECMO machine at the hospital, to save his life after he was found face down in the snow with no heartbeat. Despite temporary nerve damage and missing memories of the day, Tommy woke up without brain damage after five days in a coma and returned to endurance running nine months later.
key_points: Tommy Price and his friend Max were running a 30-mile route in freezing conditions when severe hypothermia caused Tommy's legs to seize and his heart to stop.
Keswick Mountain Rescue volunteers and medical personnel performed extensive manual CPR and delivered electric shocks before flying him to the hospital.
At the hospital, doctors used an ECMO machine to take over his heart and lung functions, and he regained consciousness after five days in an induced coma.
He suffered permanent minor nerve damage in his hands and feet, but recovered full mobility and successfully completed the London Marathon nine months later.

title: Surveys at the Ivanpah solar site in the Mojave predicted at most 32 desert tortoises, and crews then unearthed close to 1,000, halted construction for three months and spent 56 million dollars relocating them, with one juvenile carried off to an eagle nest, microchip still pinging
author: Space Daily; Brendan Brown
content:
Before the bulldozers rolled into the Ivanpah Valley, in the California Mojave just short of the Nevada line, the biologists walked the site and counted. Their first survey of the 3,500-acre footprint found 16 desert tortoises. Refined estimates pushed the likely total to a few dozen, with 32 commonly cited as the upper bound. Federal regulators wrote the permits accordingly: the $2.2 billion BrightSource solar project could relocate a maximum of 38 adult tortoises, with a hard cap of three accidental deaths per year. Exceed either number and the whole project could be shut down.
Then construction started, and the desert began handing up tortoises.
The count that would not stop
Desert tortoises are almost comically hard to survey. They spend up to 95 percent of their lives underground in burrows, and a juvenile is the size of a cookie, the color of the dirt, and silent. A walked survey samples the surface of a landscape whose inhabitants are almost all beneath it.
At Ivanpah, that sampling error detonated. As crews cleared land through 2010 and 2011, workers and monitors kept finding animals the surveys had missed, until biologists’ estimates of the site’s population reached 162 adults and 608 juveniles, roughly 770 tortoises on ground certified to hold a few dozen, and federal reviewers concluded that more than 2,300 additional juveniles lived within a couple of miles of the fences. Every discovery pushed the company closer to its federal thresholds, and in 2012 the tortoise did what almost nothing else could do to a flagship energy project: excavation work found so many animals that construction stood still for three months.
The most expensive reptiles in America
What followed became the most elaborate, and costly, tortoise rescue ever mounted. BrightSource hired teams of consulting biologists, some billed at up to $1,000 a day, to locate, excavate and move the animals under protocols negotiated line by line with state and federal agencies. The company built a tortoise nursery on site, agreed to five years of post-move monitoring, and strung some 50 miles of buried, tortoise-proof fencing at up to $50,000 per mile to keep relocated animals from burrowing straight back.
By the time the plant’s mirrors were rising, the company had spent $56 million on protecting and relocating the tortoises. Divide that by the animals actually handled and Ivanpah’s tortoises rank among the most expensive wild animals ever moved, tens of thousands of dollars a head.
The money could not buy a clean outcome. The Los Angeles Times, which chronicled the effort, catalogued the mishaps: tortoises crushed under vehicle tires, army ants swarming hatchlings in the makeshift nursery, and one small tortoise plucked from the desert and carried off to a golden eagle’s nest, the microchip embedded in its shell still pinging faintly as it receded out of range. Relocation itself is hard on the species; moved tortoises often try to walk home, and studies of past translocations have found elevated death rates from predators, exposure and stress.
Why the surveys failed
The Ivanpah undercount was not incompetence so much as the nature of the animal colliding with the nature of a deadline. Tortoise numbers fluctuate with rainfall: in dry years the animals stay sealed in their burrows and are effectively invisible, and the pre-construction surveys were walked in drought. Wetter seasons during construction brought the population to the surface just as heavy machinery arrived to meet it.
The lesson was expensive enough that it changed the industry. Later Mojave solar projects went in with multi-season surveys, bigger relocation budgets priced in from the start, and in some cases redesigned footprints. BrightSource itself had already shrunk Ivanpah by 12 percent and cut its planned power towers from seven to three during permitting, sacrificing about a tenth of its output to reduce the tortoise toll before a single mirror was installed.
The desert’s stubborn survivor
There is an irony in which species stopped the bulldozers. The desert tortoise is one of evolution’s great endurers, a lineage that watched the dinosaurs go and sat out the ice ages, capable of living a year on the water in one spring meal. What it cannot easily survive is the pace of the modern Mojave: highways, ravens subsidized by landfills, off-road traffic, and now the utility-scale build-out of the sunniest land in America, much of it prime tortoise habitat.
Ivanpah became the case study both sides cite. To solar’s critics, it is proof that renewable energy has an ecological price tag that gets paid in bulldozed habitat and six-figure animal removals. To its defenders, it is proof the system worked: the tortoises were found, the project paid, the species’ presence reshaped a two-billion-dollar build. Both readings agree on the underlying fact, which is the one the surveys got wrong. The empty-looking desert was never empty. It was full of tortoises, underground, waiting out the dry years, right up until the day the ground began to move.
summary: Pre-construction surveys at the Ivanpah solar site in the Mojave Desert predicted at most 32 desert tortoises, but construction crews ultimately unearthed close to 1,000 animals. This massive undercount halted construction for three months and forced the project to spend $56 million on an elaborate relocation effort. Despite these costly rescue measures, the translocation process and site mishaps resulted in various complications, including crushed tortoises, ant swarms, and a juvenile carried off to an eagle nest.
key_points: Initial surveys of the 3,500-acre site estimated a maximum of 32 desert tortoises, relying on samples taken during a drought when tortoises remained underground.
Construction in 2010 and 2011 revealed nearly 1,000 tortoises, forcing a three-month halt to excavation work.
BrightSource spent $56 million on protecting and relocating the animals, funding consulting biologists, a nursery, tortoise-proof fencing, and monitoring.
The rescue effort faced several mishaps, including tortoises crushed by vehicles, ant attacks in the nursery, and a microchipped juvenile taken by a golden eagle.
The massive undercount led to industry changes, prompting later Mojave solar projects to conduct multi-season surveys and increase relocation budgets.

title: The Biggest Known Galaxy Is 1.7 Million Light-Years, And We Can't Comprehend The Scale
author: Michelle Starr
content:
The Universe can pull some wild monkeyshines, especially when it comes to scale.
From giant black holes to massive sheet-like walls of galaxies, our reality is full of mind-boggling chonkers.
But a galaxy named IC 1101 is bonkers in a way that dramatically exceeds the upper end of normal.
Using the deepest observations yet of IC 1101, astronomers have made the strongest measurement to date of its physical extent, identifying the boundary of its main stellar body some 260 kiloparsecs from its center.
That makes it around 1.7 million light-years across – which makes it, according to a team led by astrophysicist Carlos Marrero de la Rosa of Spain's Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias, the largest galaxy known to date.
And the kicker? It's still growing.
"For comparison, the stellar disk of the Milky Way is roughly twenty times smaller in diameter," Marrero de la Rosa told ScienceAlert.
"Another way to picture its size is that, if IC 1101 were placed between the Milky Way and Andromeda, its main stellar body would almost bridge the space between the two galaxies."
![The Biggest Known Galaxy Is 1.7 Million Light-Years, And We Can't Comprehend The Scale](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/ic-1101-body.jpg)
IC 1101 has long been recognized as a large galaxy. It sits within a cluster of galaxies named Abell 2029 like a well-fed spider sitting in a web, glowing with the contentment that can only be expressed with trillions upon trillions of stars.
But pinning down its diameter has been something of a challenge, because the stars at the outer limits of its main body blend in with the diffuse starlight permeating the cluster around it – like the spider's legs blending in with the strands of its web, if you will.
"A galaxy does not usually have a sharp edge like a solid object. Its stars become progressively more diffuse with distance from the center," Marrero de la Rosa said.
"So the 'edge' is not the place where stars suddenly disappear, but the radius where the main body of the galaxy stops behaving as a coherent structure."
Previous observations had shown that IC 1101 was very extended, but were not able to clearly establish that edge. Because Marrero de la Rosa's PhD thesis work partly focused on the technical challenges of finding galaxy edges, the galaxy represented the perfect laboratory for testing techniques to do so.
For the new study, he and his colleagues used the 2.5-meter Isaac Newton Telescope at Spain's Roque de los Muchachos Observatory to obtain the deepest images ever taken of IC 1101.
But the hardest part came next: painstakingly removing scattered light from foreground stars and the bright concentrated light from the center of IC 1101 itself.
![The Biggest Known Galaxy Is 1.7 Million Light-Years, And We Can't Comprehend The Scale](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/sdss_legacy_int_comparison.jpg)
That part is crucial because light from bright objects can get smeared around by the telescope and atmosphere and masquerade as genuine faint material in a galaxy's outskirts.
Once they removed those effects, the team looked for changes in several properties of IC 1101 as they moved outward from its center.
At about 260 kiloparsecs, several things changed together: the distribution of light, the color of the stars, the amount of stellar mass, and even the shape and orientation of the galaxy.
Because all these independent measurements changed at roughly the same distance from the galactic center in multiple directions, the researchers interpreted this as the edge of IC 1101's main stellar body – a structure 520 kiloparsecs, or 1.7 million light-years, across.
But then something unexpected emerged.
"Once the scattered light was removed, the field became much cleaner and several very faint structures around IC 1101 became visible. Some of them are asymmetric, filamentary, or plume-like, which suggests that they may be related to past accretion events or interactions with smaller galaxies," Marrero de la Rosa explained.
"What was especially interesting was that these structures did not look like random background fluctuations. They appeared to form a complex low-surface-brightness environment around the galaxy, consistent with the idea that IC 1101 is still assembling material in its outskirts."
![The Biggest Known Galaxy Is 1.7 Million Light-Years, And We Can't Comprehend The Scale](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/08/structures.jpg)
These structures explain why the galaxy can have a coherent edge and still be growing.
The boundary the researchers found represents the edge of the main body where most of the galaxy's stars reside.
But IC 1101's reach doesn't end at that boundary. In its diffuse outskirts, stars and debris from smaller galaxies continue to accumulate, gradually adding material to the enormous system.
And, deliciously, some of those outer structures appear to line up with vast disturbances seen in the X-ray emission around IC 1101. That emission traces hot gas that, the researchers say, may retain the fingerprint of an off-axis merger with a smaller galaxy cluster a few billion years ago.
This tells us two things. It's a strong clue about how monster galaxies like IC 1101 can reach a prodigious size – and it shows that the machinery capable of building such monsters is still at work in the Universe.
"I would be cautious about saying that IC 1101 is the absolute upper limit, because the Universe may still contain other very extended systems that have not yet been studied with comparable depth and care," Marrero de la Rosa told ScienceAlert.
"But IC 1101 is currently one of the strongest observational constraints we have on how large a galaxy can become in the present-day Universe."
![Subscribe to ScienceAlert's free fact-checked newsletter](https://www.sciencealert.com/images/2026/05/FOMO-1200x628-_Dont-miss-the-next-breakthrough_-cosmic-colourful-642x336.jpg)
If they're out there, astronomers would like to identify them – because these behemoths retain records of the most extreme galactic growth histories. They grow to such enormous sizes mainly by accreting and merging with other galaxies – and the traces of those mergers are preserved in their outskirts.
The researchers plan to use their techniques to search for these giant galaxies to try to understand if IC 1101 is truly exceptional, or part of a population of similar objects that we have just not been able to identify until now.
And if it's exceptional, it may offer a window into how the Universe will continue to evolve.
"IC 1101 is, in some sense, a galaxy of the future: as time goes on, more and more massive galaxies may grow to similar sizes," Marrero de la Rosa said.
"In IC 1101, this process appears to have happened unusually efficiently, giving us a glimpse of what the future of many massive galaxies could look like."
The findings have been accepted in Astronomy & Astrophysics and are available on arXiv.
summary: Astronomers have made the most precise measurement of IC 1101, identifying the boundary of its main stellar body at about 260 kiloparsecs from its center, making it approximately 1.7 million light-years across and the largest known galaxy to date. Using deep observations from the Isaac Newton Telescope, researchers removed scattered foreground and central light to locate where the galaxy's properties change, establishing its coherent edge. Despite having this defined boundary, faint structures in its outer environment indicate that IC 1101 is still actively accumulating material and growing.
key_points: IC 1101 is currently the largest known galaxy, measuring roughly 1.7 million light-years across.
The galaxy is about twenty times larger in diameter than the Milky Way's stellar disk.
Researchers used the Isaac Newton Telescope to take deep images and removed scattered light to clearly identify the galaxy's edge.
Faint structures and debris in the outer outskirts indicate that IC 1101 is still growing by accumulating material from smaller galaxies.

title: Another eclipse over Spain on 28 August: where and how to see it
author: Christina Thykjaer
content:
Spain will turn its eyes to the sky just 16 days after the historic total solar eclipse. On 28 August a partial lunar eclipse of magnitude 0.93 will be visible across the country and will not require special eye protection.
Just 16 days after the historic total solar eclipse of 12 August, the first visible from the Iberian Peninsula in more than a century, Spain will once again be looking to the skies to witness another major astronomical event.
On 28 August there will be a partial lunar eclipse with a magnitude of 0.93, which will be visible across the country. Unlike the solar eclipse, there will be no need for special glasses or any other form of protection to enjoy this event. The National Geographic Institute (IGN) says it can be observed with the naked eye without any risk and that no special instruments will be required.
The eclipse will be particularly deep. According to the IGN, it will reach a magnitude of 0.93, which means that at its peak the Earth’s darkest shadow, known as the umbra, will cover roughly 93% of the Moon’s diameter. This figure should not be confused with the percentage of the Moon’s surface that will be darkened.
A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth moves between the Sun and the Moon and our satellite passes through the shadow cast by the planet. When only part of the Moon enters the Earth’s umbra, as will happen on 28 August, the eclipse is classified as partial.
Where will the eclipse be seen best?
The event will be visible in some of its phases from Europe, Africa, the Americas and western Asia, according to IGN data. In Spain, the partial phase will be visible from the whole country before moonset, although there will be significant differences depending on where it is observed from.
In the centre and east of the peninsula, the Balearic Islands and Melilla, the Moon will set before the partial phase ends. In the rest of the peninsula, the Canary Islands and Ceuta, moonset will occur after this phase has finished.
This makes it particularly important to look for a place with good visibility towards the horizon where the Moon will set, as well as favourable weather conditions.

![A person observes a partial solar eclipse with special protective glasses at Crosby beach in Liverpool as the moon covers part of the sun in Liverpool, England](https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/87/27/40/480x270_cmsv2_0e8deea3-9e9b-57ad-9305-7d02c34f280b-9872740.jpg) 
![A lunar eclipse will be visible in the early hours of Friday 14 March 2025 in Chicago.](https://images.euronews.com/articles/stories/09/88/45/56/480x270_cmsv2_e9c4be82-fed1-5c92-bf5e-9a0db1aa62f9-9884556.jpg)
summary: Just 16 days after a total solar eclipse, Spain will witness a partial lunar eclipse on 28 August with a magnitude of 0.93. The event will be visible across the entire country before moonset and does not require special eye protection. Observers should seek a location with good visibility toward the western horizon and favorable weather conditions.
key_points: A partial lunar eclipse will be visible across Spain on 28 August.
The eclipse will have a magnitude of 0.93, meaning the Earth's umbra will cover about 93% of the Moon's diameter.
No special glasses or instruments are required to safely view the lunar eclipse.
Visibility of the final phases will vary depending on the region before moonset occurs.

title: New book reveals preparations for Trinity nuclear test
author: Emily Seyl; Alexander McNamara
content:
![Emily Seyl's avatar](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/3vcqqXt2RMJYChMzZf7hKa.jpg) 
In the early hours of July 16, 1945, in a remote part of the New Mexico desert, a group of scientists, engineers and military personnel attended an event that would define the course of history and change a war that had ravaged much of the world for years. Moments after a giant fireball rose high into the sky, a huge shock wave thundered toward the onlooking crowd. The Trinity nuclear test had been a success.
The story of the Manhattan Project is well known. But one area that may be overlooked is the human effort involved in bringing the mission to life. In her new book "Trinity: An Illustrated History of the World’s First Atomic Test" (The University of Chicago Press, 2026), author Emily Seyl, a science writer and editor at the Los Alamos National Laboratory's National Security Research Center, uses never-before-seen photography from the laboratory’s legacy collections to highlight the physical and mental effort that went into the project.
In this excerpt, Seyl examines one of the key elements of any scientific experiment — how to successfully measure the results. She looks at how experiments were decided upon and the ways in which success would be measured, beyond the visual spectacle of a successful detonation of "the Gadget."
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/CMps2SbKPMbhUvJA2JECH8.jpg) 
The most rudimentary measure of success would, of course, be the eye test: Did the Gadget produce a nuclear explosion? Beyond the answer to this simple question, however, the detonation was also a monumental and complicated science experiment — one that naturally gave rise to as many smaller experiments as could be squeezed, sometimes impractically, into the test plans.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PFrArjZtVFhzudt4FxKbA8.jpg) 
Alongside a crowd of Trinity contributors, a robust collection of electronic and mechanical observers was stationed carefully throughout the desert to bear witness to the shot. Although deceptively rugged and nondescript, these devices were highly sophisticated, often employing first-of-their-kind technologies — invented and built by some of the world's preeminent researchers to study a first-of-its-kind event.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZYMreSRYMhsL5umiebEV58.jpg) 
After two years of leapfrogging basic nuclear studies in their rush to produce a workable device, the pioneering scientists now "yielded to temptation and conceived experiment after experiment" in anticipation of the Trinity test — much to Kenneth Bainbridge's [director of the Manhattan Project's Trinity nuclear test] alarm. In December of 1944, with base camp still under construction at the test site, a selection committee, headed by Bainbridge, had been established to evaluate what was quickly becoming a deluge of ideas.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/DwV6DkSpHA6ChjrFdwiNt7.jpg) 
The committee implemented a detailed submission process, requiring scientists to scrupulously outline the personnel and material needs associated with carrying out each idea. Proposed subtests were triaged into three categories: essential experiments, which were fully greenlit no matter the required effort or resources; desirable experiments, which were approved only if they did not interfere with work on the Gadget itself; and unnecessary (i.e., nonessential) experiments, of which only the simplest were allowed.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/eHtVPvHZCMkynkvCws46t7.jpg) 
Completing the Gadget remained the top priority. But while most of the lab continued to work feverishly on readying the test device, a significant battery of physicists, photographers, chemists, engineers, and other specialists began coming and going between Los Alamos and the Trinity site in March, as Jumbo [a containment vessel for use in case the nuclear explosion failed] faded into the background. With confidence increasing and a clear emphasis on learning everything possible about the performance of the test device, they were consumed from dawn to dusk with readying cameras and other diagnostic instrumentation to track the effects of the blast from detonation to dissipation.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/MqRXQ2e6W6EZAjiZxas5h7.jpg) 
The greatest unknown was how much energy would be released by the weapon. This value — also known as the yield — would depend on how much of the plutonium fuel underwent fission. The aim was to get as much energy from the explosion as possible.To quantify whatever success or failure awaited, scientists made plans to observe three manifestations of that energy: the amount of radiation emitted from the core (including neutrons, gamma rays, and fission fragments); the pressures and speeds of the air and ground shock waves; and the size and temperature of the fireball, which would indicate the amount of energy released as heat.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/PX5Mtd9aTFYtNTDiCxUXe7.jpg) 
With the right combination of approaches and protections, they hoped to record in several ways all effects of the explosion. If the experiments were to have any chance of capturing the various expected phenomena, however, they had to be set up close enough to absorb and record the effects while simultaneously far enough away to withstand them. Difficult decisions about siting and fortification were made harder by the fact that only rough and frequently changing estimates of the Gadget's capacity for destruction were available to serve as guideposts.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/x5RnRvGnY5h4hp9Caysad7.jpg) 
Nevertheless, scientists brought the rigor of the laboratory to the desert in dozens of clever ways. Some of the myriad devices relied on communication lines to quickly carry data back to recording instruments in bunkers. Others were programmed to send up visual signals that would be filmed by timestamped cameras placed at safer distances.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ENRLovpBdJpvptfDe5m8c7.jpg) 
Still others were purely mechanical, installed dangerously close to the blast but made of resilient materials or buried underground, the plan being to recover them in the aftermath to harvest data. Not knowing which approaches to the balancing act would turn out to be successful, they relied on overlap and redundancy to account for failure.
 ![Photo from Trinity Nuclear Test site](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/VZQFSrWkJXC5fM9KVrPua7.jpg) 
Although the cameras and instruments ultimately, and not unexpectedly, varied in their performance, the experimental program altogether would succeed in committing to history a comprehensive visual record and a trove of data, built upon the talents and toils of many.
 ![Book cover of "Trinity: An Illustrated History of the World’s First Atomic Test"](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/k4FuuP2GMgJaQNv2AcdLaA.jpg) 
"Trinity" is a stunning collection of photographs leading up to the culmination of the Manhattan Project, that captures the intensity and significance of the moment in beautiful detail — AM 
![Emily Seyl](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/3vcqqXt2RMJYChMzZf7hKa.jpg)
Emily Seyl is a science writer and editor at Los Alamos National Laboratory’s National Security Research Center.
summary: A new book by Emily Seyl, "Trinity: An Illustrated History of the World’s First Atomic Test," uses previously unseen photography to highlight the human effort and scientific preparation behind the 1945 nuclear test. Beyond verifying a successful detonation, scientists deployed a complex array of electronic, mechanical, and optical instruments to measure the blast's radiation, shock waves, and thermal output. Managing the overwhelming volume of proposed subtests required a dedicated selection committee led by Kenneth Bainbridge to triage experiments into essential, desirable, and unnecessary categories.
key_points: Emily Seyl's book highlights the physical and mental effort behind the Manhattan Project using never-before-seen photography.
A selection committee headed by Kenneth Bainbridge was established in December 1944 to triage and approve numerous proposed subtests.
Scientists planned to measure three main manifestations of energy: radiation, shock waves, and fireball size and temperature.
Researchers used redundancy, resilient materials, and strategic placement to capture data despite unpredictable destruction estimates.

title: SpaceX sends 27 Starlink satellites to orbit on 100th Falcon rocket launch of the year (video, photos)
author: Mike Wall
content:
SpaceX launched another batch of its Starlink internet satellites this morning (Aug. 22) on a milestone mission for the company's Falcon rocket family.
A Falcon 9 carrying 27 Starlink spacecraft lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California today at 3:25 a.m. EDT (0725 GMT; 12:25 a.m. local California time).
It was the 99th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 100th Falcon mission of 2026 overall. The other flight was performed by a Falcon Heavy, which lofted the telecom satellite Viasat-3 F3 in April.
 ![A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink internet satellites from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base on Aug. 22, 2026.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/ZamAtzckVKvmGo57g3Z2oM.jpg) 
Hitting the century mark at this point in the year is impressive. But SpaceX has a ways to go to equal its single-year Falcon launch record of 165, which was set in 2025. All of those were Falcon 9 missions.
The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth today as planned. It touched down about 8.5 minutes after launch in the Pacific Ocean, atop the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the ninth flight for this particular booster, which carries the designation B1100.
The 27 Starlink satellites, meanwhile, kept traveling to low Earth orbit aboard the Falcon 9's upper stage, deploying on schedule just under 62 minutes after launch.
Today's launch makes the largest-ever satellite constellation even bigger: Starlink already consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft.
 ![a stack of folded-up satellites are seen attached to their rocket's upper stage in orbit, with earth in the background](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/p7KZrawCQ7PwRZSm3QGzkY.jpg) 
As you might expect, Starlink satellites are SpaceX's most common payload; 76 of this year's 99 Falcon 9 flights have been dedicated Starlink missions.
And the number of SpaceX satellites is expected to rise considerably in the coming years. The company has said it wants to launch 100,000 of its next-gen Starlink V3 satellites and operate a constellation of one million data centers in Earth orbit. These spacecraft will fly atop SpaceX's Starship megarocket, which remains in development.
